terminology.text: The Maharashtra Forest Department's glossary uses ghat for a road with a steep gradient. An individual ghat's name meaning is not inferred just from a similar-sounding word.
terminology.locator: Glossary of local terms, printed p. xxxvi

nameNotes.text: This atlas's northern Amboli is the Trimbakeshwar-Jawhar corridor; it is not the Sawantwadi Amboli pass.
nameNotes.locator: Trimbakeshwar-Jawhar road description and northern pass inventory

significance.text: The Zilla Parishad describes the scenic Trimbakeshwar-Jawhar road, establishing a northern Maharashtra-side coastal connection.

nameNotes.text: Kasara and Thal are names for this northern gateway; neither name's etymology is established here.
nameNotes.locator: Geography introduction: Kasara or Thal Ghat

history.text: The Nasik Gazetteer describes the Thal pass as extremely difficult for loaded carts in 1841, before the improved Bombay-Agra road.
history.locator: Historical roads: 1841 and the Thal pass

significance.text: The same road account places Kasara at the foot of the Thal pass on the Bombay-Agra connection.

history.text: Maharashtra Tourism associates the region with Maratha strategic movement and older routes between the plateau and coast; no ancient date is assigned to this modern road.

forts.text: Harishchandragad is listed as a nearby historic fort. The reviewed tourism account does not establish that it guarded this exact modern road.

legends.text: For nearby Ajoba Hill, the tourism department records a Ramayana tradition connecting Sita with Valmiki's ashram. This is a neighbouring landscape tradition, not a proven event or the origin of Malshej's name.

significance.text: Government tourism identifies the pass with escarpment scenery, waterfalls and routes between the plateau and coastal region.

nameNotes.text: The Botanical Survey lists Bor and Khandala as names for the Bombay-Pune crossing.

nameMeaning.text: A nearby landmark has a documented meaning: the Poona Gazetteer translates Nag-phani as Cobra's Hood, also called Duke's Nose. This does not explain the name Bor.

history.text: The regional heritage listing dates the Karjat-Khandala railway ascent to May 1863. It is an engineering companion to the road crossing, not the construction date of today's road.
history.locator: The Bhor Ghat Ascent, report p. 6

forts.text: The Poona Gazetteer places Rajmachi north of Bor pass and explains its name as Royal Terrace. This is a documented fort association, not proof that the modern alignment passes through it.

significance.text: Bor is the documented Bombay-Pune gateway linking the Konkan lowland with the plateau.

history.text: The older Poona Gazetteer already names Tamhini at the district's southwestern corner. That geographical mention does not date the construction of the present motor road.

significance.text: The Konkan Divisional Commissioner locates the modern ghat road near Mulshi Dam and the Mangaon side, explaining its Pune-to-Raigad role.

history.text: The Satara Gazetteer dates the made Varandha pass road's construction from 1851 to 1857.

significance.text: The gazetteer identifies Varandha as an important wheeled outlet towards Mahad, crossing the Sahyadri barrier between inland markets and the coast.

nameNotes.text: Official geography reconciles Fitzgerald, Ambenali and Radtondi spellings; an explanation of the personal or place-name origin is not established here.

history.text: The Satara Gazetteer describes the Fitzgerald road as a nineteenth-century wheeled connection to Mahad. Its differing opening dates across passages are not treated here as a settled year.

forts.text: Pratapgad is explicitly associated with defending the historic Par pass. The gazetteer also describes the Fitzgerald approach; the old Par pass is not equated with every part of today's Ambenali road.

legends.text: Maharashtra Tourism records a belief connecting Pratapgad's Bhavani temple with the gifting of Shivaji's sword. It is presented as a recorded belief, not a verified historical event.
legends.locator: An Experience for Visitors: Bhavani Temple

significance.text: Official geographic accounts identify this as the Mahabaleshwar-to-Konkan connection, distinct from the neighbouring historic Par route.

history.text: The Satara Gazetteer dates construction of the Kumbharli road from 1855 to 1864, connecting the Karad side with Chiplun.

forts.text: The Satara Gazetteer describes Jangli Jayagad on a spur near Helvak. It does not establish a guarding role for this exact modern alignment.

legends.text: The gazetteer explicitly calls Tai Telin's reported possession of Jangli Jayagad in 1810 a local story. It is a nearby fort tradition, not an independently proven ghat-origin account.

significance.text: The historical road account identifies Kumbharli as a major outlet carrying inland exports towards the coast.

history.text: The Ratnagiri Gazetteer lists Amba among the main cart-road openings serving coastal trade.

forts.text: The historical pass description locates Vishalgad at the mouth of Amba's older routes, explaining a fort-road relationship without claiming an identical modern alignment.
forts.locator: Clunes account of AMBA and Vishalgad

significance.text: The same account links Amba with the Sangameshwar, Ratnagiri and Rajapur trading side.

nameNotes.text: The older gazetteer uses the spelling Anaskura; this records a historical spelling, not a translation of the name.

history.text: Anaskura is described as a main through-trade route towards Rajapur in the older Ratnagiri Gazetteer.

significance.text: Its documented trading connection helps explain why this inland-to-Rajapur corridor matters beyond today's beach itineraries.
The Gaganbawada tourism account distinguishes this branch towards Kharepatan-Rajapur from Karul's Talere-Kankavli branch.

forts.text: Gagangad is documented near Gaganbawada. The reviewed account establishes proximity, not a proven guarding role over this modern road.

significance.text: The Gaganbawada account identifies Karul's Talere-Kankavli branch separately from the Bhuibawada road towards Rajapur.

forts.text: Gagangad is the documented nearby hill fort; proximity is not presented as evidence that it guarded this exact road.

history.text: The Kolhapur Gazetteer records an artillery detachment descending Phonda around 1820, illustrating the pass's historical transport role.

forts.text: The same account places Sivgad fort by the separate Sivgad pass, near Phonda. It does not establish that the fort guarded today's Phonda alignment.

significance.text: Phonda is identified as a major historical opening from the Deccan towards Malvan.

nameNotes.text: The Savantvadi Gazetteer also calls the older Amboli route Parpoli; this is a documented alias, not a name etymology.
nameNotes.locator: Old Parpoli pass and Amboli Pass Trade

history.text: The gazetteer describes pack-bullock grain traffic over the old Parpoli route and a reversal towards imported food during the 1876-77 famine.

significance.text: This account connects the pass with the Vengurla trading network, giving the coastal approach an economic history as well as a landscape story.

history.text: The Maharashtra government's 2024 monument schedule attributes Pargad's construction to Shivaji in 1674 and names Raiba Malusare as its first killedar.

forts.text: The notification explicitly says Pargad monitored Portuguese movement in Goa. This establishes a regional watch role, not that every modern road bend is historical.
forts.locator: English Schedule: purpose of the fort

significance.text: The same legal schedule locates the fort at Mirvel, connecting the atlas's corridor name with a documented borderland monument.

history.text: Maharashtra's 2021-22 hydrology report lists multiple Tillari projects, including Main, Forebay and Interstate; the road is not assumed to have the same construction date as a dam.
history.locator: Kokan annual hydrological status report, p. 100

significance.text: PWD's published road inventory identifies the Kolhapur-Chandgad-Tillari-Dodamarg corridor, a distinct link to the southern Konkan.

history.text: Goa PWD's 2021 charter records the Sankhali-Chorla connection. That is dated documentary evidence, not a claim about when the pass was first used.

significance.text: The charter identifies a separate Goa-side approach through Sankhali, distinguishing Chorla from the Anmod-Ponda corridor.

history.text: A March 2025 ministerial answer describes the Goa-Belagavi connection via Anmod as NH748. No old-pass founding date is inferred.

significance.text: The ministry identifies Anmod as part of the Goa-Belagavi highway, while Goa PWD documents the Anmod-Ponda section.

nameNotes.text: Official forest records use Anashi as a range name; the reviewed records do not establish the word's etymology.

history.text: The 1961 North Kanara district handbook identifies Anashi on the Belgaum-Kadra PWD road, providing a dated road-history reference.

significance.text: The documented Kadra-side connection explains this atlas's southern approach through neighbouring Karnataka rather than an invented direct Maharashtra pass.
